subtopic_detail: Confusion and coarse tremor in a long term lithium user whose serum level is within the therapeutic range
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 72 year old woman brought in by her son. She has taken lithium for twenty years for bipolar affective disorder and has never had a manic relapse.

For three days she has been unsteady, has slurred her words and has been muddled about the day of the week, and this morning she could not manage her own kitchen. She had four days of vomiting and diarrhoea last week after a family gathering and has been drinking little. Her general practitioner started perindopril for hypertension five weeks ago. On examination she has a coarse irregular tremor of both hands, myoclonic jerks in her legs, and an unsteady wide gait. There is no fever, no rigidity, no clonus and no rash, and her neck is supple.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.94 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 maintenance), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 78), sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), estimated glomerular filtration rate 38 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone 3.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatine kinase 140 U/L (less than 200)
data_table.Examination: Coarse irregular tremor, leg myoclonus, wide based ataxic gait, no rigidity or clonus, no neck stiffness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue lithium at the usual dose because the serum concentration is not in the toxic range
options.rationale: Chronic toxicity produces marked neurological features at concentrations that look acceptable, because tissue levels exceed serum levels after years of treatment. A reassuring number is the classic trap in the long term user (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Prescribe benztropine for the tremor and arrange outpatient review of her lithium level next week
options.rationale: An anticholinergic does not treat lithium induced tremor and worsens delirium in an older patient, and outpatient follow up leaves an unsafe woman at home. Anticholinergics treat drug induced parkinsonism, which is not the picture here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Withhold lithium, rehydrate with intravenous sodium chloride and monitor levels and renal function
options.rationale: Volume depletion with a new angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor has reduced lithium clearance and produced chronic toxicity, so cessation with isotonic rehydration to restore renal excretion is the treatment. Serial levels, electrolytes and neurological assessment then determine whether extracorporeal removal becomes necessary (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Arrange immediate haemodialysis on the basis of her neurological signs and impaired renal function
options.rationale: Dialysis is reserved for severe toxicity with markedly elevated concentrations, seizures, depressed conscious state, or failure to fall with supportive care and renal impairment. Starting with rehydration allows most chronic cases to clear without it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Treat her for neuroleptic malignant syndrome with dantrolene and supportive cooling measures
options.rationale: That syndrome features fever, lead pipe rigidity and a markedly raised creatine kinase, all absent here, and she takes no antipsychotic. Its overlap with lithium toxicity is the tremor and confusion, which is why the rigidity and creatine kinase are the discriminating findings (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is divided into acute overdose, acute on chronic, and chronic toxicity, and it is the chronic form that catches clinicians out because neurological features dominate at concentrations barely above the therapeutic range. The drug is cleared entirely by the kidney and handled like sodium, so any state that reduces glomerular filtration or increases proximal sodium reabsorption raises the level, including dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea, heart failure and a hot climate. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, thiazides and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are the classic interacting medicines. Management is cessation, isotonic fluid to restore clearance, correction of the precipitant and serial monitoring, with extracorporeal removal for severe or refractory cases. A minority of patients are left with persistent cerebellar dysfunction, which is why early recognition matters.
key_points: Chronic toxicity causes marked neurological signs at near therapeutic serum concentrations
Dehydration, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, thiazides and non steroidal drugs are common precipitants
Isotonic sodium chloride restores renal clearance and is the mainstay of treatment
Dialysis is for severe toxicity, seizures, coma or failure of levels to fall
Absent rigidity with a normal creatine kinase argues against neuroleptic malignant syndrome
explanation.pearls: Recheck the lithium level and renal function within five to seven days of starting any angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor, thiazide or regular non steroidal anti inflammatory drug, since these interactions can raise concentrations by a quarter or more within a fortnight.

subtopic_detail: Frequent prolonged attacks with normal video telemetry captured during a typical event
stem:
You are the neuropsychiatry registrar reviewing a 26 year old woman referred after four admissions this year. She has three to five attacks a week in which she falls, shakes and is unresponsive for eight to twelve minutes.

During a typical attack captured on video telemetry this week, her eyes were tightly closed with resistance to opening, her head moved from side to side, the shaking waxed and waned in amplitude, and she was talking within thirty seconds of it stopping. The electroencephalogram showed normal awake rhythms throughout the event and afterwards. A venous lactate taken fifteen minutes after the attack was normal. She has taken levetiracetam and lamotrigine at therapeutic doses without any change in frequency. She discloses a history of childhood sexual abuse and has never been offered psychological treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Video electroencephalogram during a typical event shows normal awake rhythms with no ictal correlate, venous lactate 1.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) at 15 minutes post event, magnetic resonance imaging of brain normal, levetiracetam and lamotrigine within therapeutic ranges

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add a third antiepileptic drug and titrate it to the maximum tolerated dose over eight weeks
options.rationale: Two adequately dosed antiepileptic drugs have failed and the recorded event had no electrographic correlate, so further antiepileptic therapy adds adverse effects without prospect of benefit. A third agent is the correct step in genuinely refractory epilepsy with recorded ictal discharges (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Instruct the emergency department to give intravenous levetiracetam whenever an attack lasts over five minutes
options.rationale: Treating these events as status epilepticus exposes her to sedation, intubation and intensive care admission for a non epileptic process, which is one of the major iatrogenic harms in this condition. Parenteral loading is reserved for electrographically confirmed prolonged seizures (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Repeat ambulatory electroencephalography over a week before accepting the telemetry findings as valid
options.rationale: Video telemetry capturing a habitual attack is the diagnostic standard and an ambulatory study is less informative, so repeating testing simply delays treatment. Further recording is justified only when the captured event was not typical of her usual attacks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Explain the diagnosis to her carefully and refer for psychological therapy while withdrawing the antiepileptics
options.rationale: A habitual event recorded without electrographic change establishes dissociative seizures, and the way the diagnosis is communicated is itself therapeutic because acceptance predicts outcome. Structured psychological therapy is the treatment with the best evidence, and antiepileptic drugs are withdrawn gradually once epilepsy has been excluded (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Refer her to an epilepsy surgery program for evaluation of a possible frontal lobe seizure focus
options.rationale: Frontal lobe seizures are the classic mimic because they are brief, bizarre and may have no scalp correlate, but they last seconds to two minutes and are stereotyped rather than waxing and waning over ten minutes. Her prolonged fluctuating events with immediate recovery do not fit that pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Dissociative seizures account for a substantial minority of patients referred to epilepsy monitoring units and are frequently misdiagnosed for years, during which patients accumulate antiepileptic drugs, emergency intubations and injury. Semiological pointers include prolonged duration, waxing and waning motor activity, side to side head movement, eye closure with resistance, ictal weeping, memory for the event and rapid reorientation afterwards, while a normal post event lactate and prolactin add supportive evidence. None of these features is individually diagnostic, so video electroencephalography during a habitual attack remains the reference standard. Communication of the diagnosis is the intervention with the greatest immediate effect, and a script that affirms the attacks are real, names the condition and explains the mechanism without implying fabrication improves engagement. Cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for these seizures is the best supported treatment, with antiepileptic drugs withdrawn under supervision.
key_points: Video electroencephalography during a habitual event is the diagnostic standard
Prolonged waxing and waning attacks with eye closure and rapid recovery favour a dissociative mechanism
A normal post event lactate supports the diagnosis but is not by itself sufficient
How the diagnosis is explained strongly influences whether treatment works
Cognitive behavioural therapy is the treatment of choice and antiepileptics are withdrawn gradually
explanation.pearls: Venous lactate rises within minutes of a generalised tonic clonic seizure and typically exceeds 2.5 mmol/L when measured in the first 30 minutes, so a normal value taken promptly after a prolonged convulsive event argues strongly against an epileptic mechanism.

subtopic_detail: Detailed recurrent visual hallucinations with fluctuating attention and mild parkinsonism in an older man
stem:
You are the old age psychiatry registrar seeing a 76 year old man with his daughter. Over twelve months he has become forgetful, and his daughter describes days when he follows a conversation normally and days when he stares blankly for hours.

He sees small children playing in the corner of the lounge room several times a week, describes their clothing in detail, and is puzzled rather than frightened by them. His writing has become small and his walking slower, though he has no tremor. For several years he has shouted and thrashed during sleep and once struck his wife while dreaming. He has had no falls, no urinary symptoms and no fevers. His mid stream urine is clear, his medications are perindopril and atorvastatin only, and his mini mental state examination score is 23 out of 30 with impaired attention and visuospatial tasks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg lying and 126/72 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mild symmetrical bradykinesia and rigidity without tremor, mini mental state examination 23 out of 30 with impaired attention and pentagon copying, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits, mid stream urine shows no growth, computed tomography of brain shows generalised atrophy without infarction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his hallucinations?

options.text: Prescribe regular haloperidol at a low dose and review his response in the clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics carry the highest risk of severe sensitivity reactions in this condition, with irreversible parkinsonism, autonomic instability and death reported after single doses. Haloperidol retains a role in hyperactive delirium from another cause, not here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start low dose risperidone and titrate the dose against the frequency of the visual phenomena
options.rationale: Risperidone has substantial dopamine blockade and produces the same sensitivity reaction, and it also carries the increased mortality seen with antipsychotics in dementia. It is the agent with the most evidence for aggression in Alzheimer disease, which is a different clinical problem (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence olanzapine at night to address both his hallucinations and his disturbed sleep pattern
options.rationale: Sedating him overnight does not treat the underlying disorder and risks the same sensitivity reaction alongside falls and further cognitive decline. Sleep disturbance in this condition is better managed by treating the sleep behaviour disorder specifically (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Use quetiapine as the antipsychotic least likely to worsen his movement disorder over time
options.rationale: Quetiapine is the least antidopaminergic option and is sometimes used when psychosis is dangerous and untreatable otherwise, but evidence for benefit is weak and it still carries the mortality signal. It is a fallback after a cholinesterase inhibitor has failed, not a first choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Modify the home environment and start rivastigmine, avoiding antipsychotic medication altogether
options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder identify Lewy body dementia, in which cholinesterase inhibitors reduce hallucinations and improve attention. Antipsychotics are avoided because up to half of patients have a severe sensitivity reaction that can be fatal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is defined by dementia plus core features of fluctuating cognition with variation in attention and alertness, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, and spontaneous parkinsonism. It is commonly mistaken for Alzheimer disease with behavioural symptoms or for delirium, and the consequence of that error is prescription of an antipsychotic. Severe sensitivity reactions occur in a large minority and include worsening parkinsonism, impaired consciousness, autonomic instability and a syndrome resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with substantially increased mortality. Cholinesterase inhibitors are unusually effective in this dementia, improving hallucinations, apathy and attention. Sleep behaviour disorder is managed with environmental safety measures and melatonin or clonazepam, and orthostatic hypotension needs non pharmacological measures before drugs are added.
key_points: Fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and sleep behaviour disorder define the syndrome
Antipsychotic sensitivity affects up to half of patients and can be fatal
Cholinesterase inhibitors reduce hallucinations and improve attention in this dementia specifically
Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder often precedes cognitive symptoms by years
Quetiapine is a reluctant fallback only when psychosis is dangerous and other measures fail
explanation.pearls: Ask every patient with new visual hallucinations whether they act out their dreams, since rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder can precede the cognitive syndrome by a decade and is the single most useful pointer away from Alzheimer disease.

subtopic_detail: Agitation and racing thoughts emerging five weeks after an antidepressant was added for bipolar depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 31 year old woman with bipolar II disorder, diagnosed after two clear hypomanic episodes and multiple depressive episodes. Her general practitioner started sertraline five weeks ago for a depressive episode and increased it a fortnight ago. She takes no mood stabiliser.

She says her mood is as low as ever and she cries daily, but she now cannot sit still, her thoughts race so fast she cannot hold a conversation, and she has slept three hours a night for a week without feeling tired. She is irritable with her family and has spent two evenings cleaning the house until dawn. She denies grandiosity, has no psychotic symptoms and has no thoughts of self harm. She uses no alcohol or other drugs, and her thyroid function and full blood examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Restless with psychomotor agitation, pressured speech at times, mood described as low with an irritable and reactive affect, no psychotic features, insight retained
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood examination and electrolytes within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her treatment?

options.text: Cease the sertraline and start quetiapine, with close review of her mood and sleep
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can precipitate a mixed state, recognisable here as depressive mood with agitation, racing thoughts and reduced sleep need, and withdrawal of the antidepressant is the first move. Quetiapine has the strongest evidence of the agents effective across bipolar depression and mixed features (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose further because her depressive symptoms have not yet responded
options.rationale: Escalating an antidepressant that has produced activation worsens the mixed state and increases the risk of a full manic switch. Dose escalation is appropriate for a partial response in unipolar depression without activation (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Add lamotrigine and continue the sertraline while the lamotrigine is slowly titrated upwards
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has a role in preventing bipolar depression but requires weeks of slow titration for rash risk and does nothing for the acute mixed presentation, and continuing the antidepressant maintains the driver. It is a maintenance rather than an acute option (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add lithium at a standard dose while maintaining her current antidepressant treatment unchanged
options.rationale: Lithium is a sound long term choice for her illness but leaving the antidepressant in place allows the activation to continue while the level is titrated over weeks. Adding a mood stabiliser without removing the precipitant treats around the problem (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Prescribe a hypnotic for her insomnia and reassess her symptoms in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: Reduced need for sleep in a mixed state is a symptom of the mood disturbance rather than primary insomnia, and a four week interval is unsafe given the risk of escalation. Hypnotics may be used briefly alongside definitive treatment, not instead of it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Mixed features occur when depressive and manic symptoms are present at the same time, and they are common in bipolar II disorder, frequently precipitated or worsened by antidepressant monotherapy. The clue is that the patient describes persistent low mood while displaying agitation, racing thoughts, irritability and reduced sleep need, and the reduced need for sleep rather than an inability to sleep is the key distinction from depressive insomnia. Mixed states carry a higher suicide risk than pure depression and often respond poorly to antidepressants, so guidelines advise stopping the antidepressant and using an agent with evidence across both poles. Quetiapine, olanzapine and some other second generation agents are used acutely, with lithium and lamotrigine playing larger roles in maintenance. Frequent review is required until sleep and agitation settle.
key_points: Depressive mood with agitation, racing thoughts and reduced sleep need indicates a mixed state
Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can precipitate mixed or manic states
Reduced need for sleep, rather than inability to sleep, marks the manic component
Mixed states carry a higher suicide risk than pure depressive episodes
Lamotrigine and lithium are maintenance agents and are too slow for the acute mixed picture
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the patient feels tired the next morning after a short night, because feeling refreshed on three hours of sleep points to a manic component and changes the treatment away from antidepressants entirely.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Four months of memory complaints with prominent distress and early morning waking after a bereavement
stem:
You are the geriatrician assessing a 72 year old retired accountant referred with memory loss. His wife died five months ago and his daughter dates the change to the weeks that followed.

He reports his memory in detail and with obvious distress, saying he is a burden and that his mind has gone. During cognitive testing he answers do not know to most questions without attempting them, yet later recalls the name of the ward clerk and the route he took to the clinic. He wakes at four each morning and has lost 6 kg without dieting. He has stopped attending bowls and no longer reads. His gait, tone and reflexes are normal, there are no hallucinations, and his mini mental state examination is 25 out of 30 with variable effort across items.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 per minute, blood pressure 134/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, restricted affect, no focal neurological signs, normal gait and tone
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging of brain shows mild generalised atrophy appropriate for age with no hippocampal predominance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start donepezil now and repeat cognitive testing again in six months to assess his trajectory
options.rationale: A cholinesterase inhibitor treats established Alzheimer disease and would neither address his mood syndrome nor clarify the diagnosis. Starting it first risks anchoring on dementia and leaving a treatable depression untreated (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Treat the depressive episode and repeat formal cognitive assessment once his mood has responded
options.rationale: A subacute onset dated to a bereavement, prominent self reproach, early morning waking, weight loss and do not know responses with preserved incidental recall point to cognitive impairment driven by depression, which improves with treatment of the mood disorder. Reassessing cognition after response is essential because a substantial proportion of these patients later develop a true dementia and need ongoing follow up (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Refer him for fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography to define the pattern of hypometabolism
options.rationale: Functional imaging is reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain dementia after treatable causes have been addressed, and depression itself alters metabolic patterns. Using it now would produce a result that is difficult to interpret (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Attribute his presentation to normal grief and arrange bereavement counselling with review in three months
options.rationale: Grief does not typically produce pervasive worthlessness, marked weight loss, psychomotor retardation and functional collapse, which mark a depressive episode requiring treatment. Counselling alone would leave a treatable and potentially dangerous illness unaddressed (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Commence a low dose antipsychotic to address his belief that he is a burden on his family
options.rationale: A sense of being a burden is a depressive cognition rather than a delusion in the absence of fixed unshakeable false beliefs, and antipsychotics increase mortality in older people with cognitive impairment. Antipsychotic augmentation is considered only for psychotic depression (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Depression in older people frequently presents with cognitive impairment, and distinguishing it from an early dementia is one of the recurring diagnostic problems of old age medicine. Features favouring a mood driven picture include a relatively short and datable history, a patient who complains vigorously about memory rather than minimising it, do not know responses with preserved recall when off guard, prominent self reproach and biological symptoms such as early morning waking and weight loss. Neurodegenerative disease more often produces a gradual course, confabulation or minimisation, impaired recognition memory and a hippocampal predominant pattern on imaging. Effective antidepressant treatment usually improves the cognitive performance substantially, though not always to a normal level. Longitudinal follow up remains essential because a large minority of these patients convert to dementia within a few years, so the two conditions are best thought of as overlapping rather than mutually exclusive.
key_points: Datable subacute onset with prominent complaint of memory loss favours a mood driven picture
Do not know responses with preserved incidental recall are characteristic
Early morning waking, weight loss and self reproach support a depressive episode
Treat the depression first, then repeat formal cognitive assessment
A substantial minority later develop dementia, so follow up is required regardless of response
explanation.pearls: Repeat formal cognitive testing about three months after a full antidepressant response, since performance that fails to improve at that point substantially raises the probability of an underlying neurodegenerative process.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
